'''Walter Gröbli''' (23 September 1852 – 26 June 1903) was a Swiss [[mathematician]].

== Life and work ==
His father, [[Issak Gröbli]], was an industrial who was invented a [[St. Gallen embroidery#Further developments|shuttle embroidery machine]] in 1863, and his old brother is credited to have introduced the invention in the [[United States]].{{sfn | Aref | Rott | Thomann | 1992 | p=2 }} Walter Gröbli was more interested in mathematics than in embroidery{{sfn | Eminger | 2015 | p=106 }} and he studied from 1871 to 1875 at the [[ETH Zurich|Polytechnicum of Zürich]] under [[Hermann Schwarz]] and [[Heinrich Martin Weber]].{{sfn | Aref | Rott | Thomann | 1992 | pp=2–3 }} Then Gröbli studied at [[university of Berlin]] and he was awarded a doctorate in the [[university of Göttingen]] (1877).

The following six years, Gröbli was assistant of [[Ferdinand Georg Frobenius|Frobenius]] in Polytechnicum of Zürich. In 1883 he was elected mathematics professor in the ''Gymnasium'' of [[Zürich]].{{sfn | Aref | Rott | Thomann | 1992 | p=18 }} Despite his mathematical talent he did not follow a research career, he was happy to be a schoolmaster.{{sfn | Eminger | 2015 | p=107 }}

His other main passion was mountaineering. He died with other three colleagues on a mountain accident climbing the [[Piz Blas]].{{sfn | Eminger | 2015 | p=108 }}

The only work known by Gröbli was his doctoral thesis dissertation. It deals about three vortex motion, four vortex motion having an axis of symmetry and <math>2n</math> vortex motion having <math>n</math> symmetry axes.{{sfn | Aref | Rott | Thomann | 1992 | pp=9–10 }} This work is a classical in [[History of fluid mechanics#Developments in vortex dynamics|vortex dynamics]] literature.{{sfn | Meleshko | Aref | 2007 | p=222 }}
